sentences.text: Calyptosuchus was an extinct reptile that lived during the Late Triassic in North America.
This animal was heavily armored and possessed a pig-like snout adapted for uprooting plants.

Its armor consisted of rows of osteoderms—bony plates embedded in the skin—where each row aligned with a single vertebra and featured four dorsal plates. The outer plates were small and squarish, while broader inner plates covered most of the back, giving the creature a boxy appearance.
Unlike some other armored reptiles, the osteoderms of Calyptosuchus were not entirely fused.
Scientists have recorded 45 fossil occurrences of this genus.
The genus was named by Long and Ballew in 1985 based on a partial shell with a spine and pelvis discovered in 1931 by Ermin Cowles Case in the Tecovas Formation of west Texas.
In a 1932 article, the discoverer initially assigned the specimen to the group Phytosauria.
Calyptosuchus had two very robust sacral vertebrae that were not fused, unlike those of desmatosuchians.
The tail featured at least seventeen caudal vertebrae with very tall neural spines and low-attached ribs.
While earlier publications treated Calyptosuchus as a synonym of Stagonolepis, recent research has determined it is a distinct genus.

The distinction from Stagonolepis is supported by the discovery of additional material of the same species, including a dentary bone, a possible maxilla, other neck and trunk vertebrae, a femur, a tibia, and extra osteoderms.
The genus was established by Long and Ballew in 1985 and belongs to the family Stagonolepididae, the subfamily Stagonolepidinae, and the parent group Desmatosuchinae.
Calyptosuchus lived from the Carnian to the Norian stages, between 237 and 205.7 million years ago.

The only skull fragment certainly assigned to Calyptosuchus is a dentary bone, as no other cranial bones have been definitively linked to it. This preserved dentary bone includes a middle section with an edentulous patch at the front and nine dental alveoli at the rear.
